headline: AI company destroys antique books post-scan, citing efficiency and scale for digital archives
summary: A 'Senior Legacy Media Completion Specialist' details his role in shredding and burning priceless antique books after they are digitized for AI training, a practice the company defends as an efficiency move.
details: A Hacker News post by an individual dubbed 'Book Doug' reveals his job as a 'Senior Legacy Media Completion Specialist,' which involves destroying priceless antique books after they've been scanned for generative AI.

The process begins with shearing off the book spines and separating pages, which are then run through large machines. These machines allow AI to 'absorb every sentence ever written' for training purposes.

After scanning, the decimated remains are brought to Doug, who uses industrial shredders and a 'giant burn pit' for their final destruction. This practice is framed within the company's 'founder-led culture' as a focus on 'scale and efficiency.'

Doug describes the older books as his favorite, noting their rich history, thick leather covers, and gold lettering. He contrasts their original state as 'treasured record of human thought' with their post-scan form: 'twelve searchable megabytes' and paper strips.

When asked if he feels bad, Doug explains that rarity is an 'inventory problem.' He argues that making a single copy 'infinitely reproducible and immediately unavailable to anyone without a subscription' is the efficient solution.

The company also incorporates recycling, with some of the processed pulp becoming cardboard. This cardboard may eventually be used to ship more books to the company for the same digitization and destruction process.

headline_marked: [[21 Bytes Can Crash FFmpeg]]: AI-assisted fuzzer finds bug years of audits missed
headline: 21 Bytes Can Crash FFmpeg: AI-assisted fuzzer finds bug years of audits missed
summary: A critical division-by-zero bug in FFmpeg, triggered by a mere 21 bytes, was discovered by an AI-assisted fuzzer, highlighting a new era in vulnerability detection.
details: A file just 21 bytes long, containing four zero bytes at a specific offset, can crash any FFmpeg-based application that processes it. This critical vulnerability is a division-by-zero error in code that has been present for years, despite FFmpeg being one of the most fuzzed codebases globally.

The bug was discovered by Darío Clavijo using an AI-assisted fuzzer, which he dubbed a "vibecoded fuzzer." This finding has sparked significant debate on Hacker News about the changing economics of bug discovery, as AI increasingly aids security researchers.

The vulnerability resides in `libavformat/vpk.c`, the demuxer for Sony PS2 VPK audio files, an obscure container format. The crash chain leads to a division by zero when `nb_channels` is zero, causing immediate application termination.

A two-line fix has been suggested to guard against `nb_channels <= 0` at the top of `vpk_read_packet`, returning `AVERROR_INVALIDDATA`. Interestingly, a nearly identical guard for this exact division was proposed in November 2024 but never landed on the critical path.

This was not an isolated incident. The same fuzzer also documented a second high-rated FFmpeg finding: a 46-byte input that triggers an `av_assert0(0)` in `libavcodec/decode.c` through the subtitle decoder path. Two significant crashes were found in one week of fuzzing.

The fuzzer, published on GitHub as `fuzzer-tool`, is a sophisticated coverage-guided binary fuzzer. It features 147 mutation operators, 14 scheduler modules, AFL-style forkserver execution, and shared-memory edge coverage, demonstrating advanced engineering rather than a simple AI script.

The true lesson lies in the human-AI collaboration. While AI wrote much of the fuzzer's code, human-imposed structure, discipline, and rigorous triage processes – detailed in files like AGENTS.md – were crucial. This combination of "vibecoding with guardrails" proved highly effective in finding complex bugs.
